Putin watches Russian navy drills off Russia's Sakhalin Island Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 13/08/2026 - 13:00 GMT+2 Russia's President Vladimir Putin observed naval exercises off Sakhalin Island on Thursday before travelling to the disputed Kuril Islands, prompting a strong protest from Japan. … More Footage released by Russian state television showed President Vladimir Putin aboard the missile cruiser Varyag, the flagship of the Pacific Fleet, watching live‑fire naval exercises and an underwater explosion off Russia’s Far East. He later travelled to one of the archipelago's four main islands, marking the first visit to the Kurils by a Russian president since Dmitry Medvedev went there in 2010. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi described the visit as "absolutely unacceptable" , saying the islands were an inherent part of Japan. Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi also summoned Russia's ambassador in Tokyo to lodge a formal protest, warning that the visit could further damage already strained relations. The Kuril Islands have been disputed by Russia and Japan since 1945, when the Soviet Union seized the archipelago. Home to around 20,000 Russians, the islands are strategically important to Moscow for their military position and access to the Pacific, while the surrounding waters and nearby Sakhalin are rich in fishing, oil and gas. Putin’s visit and the naval drills reinforce Russia’s territorial claims and military presence in the region, sending a clear message to Japan and its Western allies. https://telex.hu/sport/2026/08/30/ferfi-.text: Menü Kereső Öttusa-vb: Koleszár nyolcadik, Szép tizenkettedik lett a 112 fős mezőnyből Sport Bakró-Nagy Ferenc Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Koleszár Mihály a nyolcadik, Szép Balázs a 12. helyen végzett az öttusázók kínai világbajnokságán, Kujjangban. A 112 fős férfi mezőny selejtezője két napon át tartott, mert eső miatt az akadályversenyt és a kombinált számot szerdáról csütörtökre tették át. A magyarok közül Koleszár és Szép jutott tovább, Bőhm Csaba és Tárkányi Zsombor – aki kedden bronzérmet nyert Guzi Blankával vegyes váltóban – kiesett. A pénteki elődöntőt mindkét versenyben maradt magyar öttusázó sikerrel vette, így a vasárnapi 18-as fináléban is szerepelhetett. A tavaly Eb-ezüstérmes Koleszár a csütörtöki rangsoroló vívásban 13 győzelmet aratott, emiatt a döntős mezőnyben csak a 15. volt, így neki a táblán már a nyolcaddöntőért is vívnia kellett. Az első mérkőzését 4-3-ra megnyerte az egyiptomi Mutaz Mohamed ellen, másodjára viszont 5-3-ra kikapott a dél-koreai Szeo Csangvantól, így a 15. helyen fejezte be az első számot. Az akadálypályán viszont jelentősen javított, 21.76 másodperccel a leggyorsabb volt, ezzel a tizedik helyre lépett előre. Egyedül a szám világcsúcstartója, az egyiptomi Mohamed el-Askar lehetett volna veszélyes rá, de az egyik függeszkedő szakasznál leesett, így ott ismételni kényszerült. A 25 méteres mobil medencében Koleszár 56.63 másodperc alatt úszta le a 100 métert, ezzel a 11. legjobb eredményt érte el, és az öt lövészettel megszakított 5x600 méteres futást a tizedik helyről kezdhette meg. Körülötte kis különbségekkel követték egymást a versenyzők, a dobogó viszont 32 másodpercre volt. Koleszárnak akadt kiváló lövősorozata, de olyan is, amelynél vesztett értékes időt a lőállásban, emiatt jelentősen nem tudott előre lépni, két pozíciót azonban így is javított. A kombinált számban 10:45.38 perccel az ötödik legjobb eredményt érte el. A 2024-ben vb-ezüstérmes, olimpiai tizedik helyezett Szép a körvívást 23 sikeres asszóval fejezte be, így a táblán az első kiemelt volt. A 16 között 5-0-ra lépte le a francia Ugo Fleurot-t, a negyeddöntőben 5-3-ra verte a kínai Ma Jü-angot, a következő körben ugyanennyire az egyiptomi Mohanad Sabant, a döntőben pedig 5-2-re kikapott el-Askartól. Az akadálypályán viszont a többiekhez képest lassan ért végig, 35.75 másodpercével 17. lett, ami azt jelentette, hogy a 13. pozícióba csúszott vissza. Úszásban nem tudott javítani, 57.58 másodperccel a 15. eredményt érte el, és 14. volt a kombinált szám rajtjánál, nyolc másodpercre Koleszártól. Csapattársához hasonlóan – kissé egyenetlenül – lőtt, de ő is jó tempóban futott, ezzel kettőt előre tudott lépni. Az összetett számban a hetedik legjobb volt 10:46.38 perccel. Győzött a cseh Matej Lukes, és a dobogóra még az orosz Jegor Gromadszkij, valamint Szeo állhatott fel. Csapatban az oroszok nyertek, az ezüst az egyiptomiaknak, a bronz a franciáknak jutott. Ez a három csapat szerepelt legalább három versenyzővel a döntőben. A magyarok a hatodik helyen zártak Bőhm Csaba selejtezős eredményével kiegészülve. Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAP View image in fullscreen Fuel prices are rising again in Australia, with petrol nearing $2.10 a litre and diesel passing $2.50. Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAP Australian economy Analysis The RBA hoped this year’s three interest rate rises would tame inflation – but nothing is going their way Patrick Commins Economics editor The breakdown of the US-Iran ceasefire, rising oil prices and the explosion in data centre investment are making the central bank’s task harder Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Wed 9 Sep 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 11.01 EDT Share For five years the Reserve Bank has been trying to wrangle inflation back to its 2.5% target, and for years it has essentially failed. The result is a cost of living crisis that has generated intense community grievance. The RBA’s deputy governor, Andrew Hauser, acknowledged as much on the ABC’s 7:30 report on Tuesday. “People are furious about inflation,” Hauser said. “Inflation has been above target for a long period of time and at some point we will have to say, ‘That is long enough’.” Inflation graph Are we at that point? Not yet, said Hauser, even as he hinted we are getting closer every day. The RBA’s nine-member board had hoped this year’s three interest rate hikes would be enough to bend the arc of inflation slowly back to reach 2.5% by the end of next year. But nothing is going their way. The latest blow is the complete breakdown of the US-Iran ceasefire, with escalating tit-for-tat strikes on oil tankers and infrastructure in and around the strait of Hormuz. The global oil benchmark has risen above $US100 a barrel for the first time since July. Fuel prices are tracking higher once again, with unleaded approaching $2.10 a litre and diesel passing $2.50. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Then there is this year’s sudden explosion in datacentre investment . That has heaped pressure on a construction sector already struggling to get the materials and labour it needs to build the massive pipeline of work to build homes, roads and rails. Households are complaining a lot and feeling depressed, but there’s still a surprising lot of spending happening, which is keeping consumption growth ticking along. Meanwhile, Australia’s productivity performance – the thing that could make it easier for the economy to grow without pushing inflation up – remains flat. Investors and an increasing number of economists believe we are approaching that point when the RBA has to say “enough is enough” and act more aggressively to get price rises back under control. Financial markets are pricing in more than a 70% chance of another rate hike on 29 September, and even the chance of a second by the end of the year. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “Of course we could raise interest rates sharply,” Hauser said. “We could do it tomorrow. We could no longer take seriously the full employment part of our objective [and say] we’re gonna bring inflation down come hell or high water.” Here Hauser is pointing out that the RBA has not been asleep at the wheel, but has been making a conscious calculation. Since mid-2021, annual inflation has only been below 3% for one year. On the other hand, unemployment has been below 5% for almost all of that time – a labour market record unmatched in modern Australia history. “The reason as a board we have decided to take it slowly is to preserve as many jobs in this country as we could,” Hauser said, and not for the first time. But the balance is starting to shift. “We have one big problem, and that’s inflation,” he said. “Inflation is too high, that’s why we raised interest rates three times at the beginning of this year. The question now, frankly, for us is have we done enough, or is more needed.” Explore more on these topics Australian economy Reserve Bank of Australia Inflation Interest rates analysis Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story High-end property hit by steepest price falls as affordable end of Australia’s housing market proves resilient Australia’s economy limps along, but the RBA should take a closer look before raising interest rates again House prices could fall 10%, analysts predict, as fourth interest rate hike looms Why the horror warnings about Australia’s ‘collapsing’ housing market are absurd – and very much in bad faith Full Story Greg Jericho on One Nation’s superannuation ‘sugar hit’ – Full Story podcast Fears grow for fourth rate hike after Australia sees higher-than-expected July inflation Australia’s housing prices are trending down. http://www.heraldglobe.com/news/27932220.text: India, V4 countries agree to deepen political, economic and defence ties; Jaishankar announces annual FM meetings, business forum ANI 22 Sep 2026, 02:59 GMT+10 New York [US], September 22 (ANI): External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar said India and the four Visegrad Group (V4) countries (Poland, Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic) have agreed to deepen cooperation in political, economic, technology, defence and people-to-people ties. Jaishankar's comments following the first V4 and India Foreign Ministers' Meeting on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly. Speaking to the media after the meeting, Jaishankar said the gathering was a "new historic occasion" and announced plans for annual meetings of foreign ministers as well as an annual business forum. "Since India's relationship with the European Union itself is deepening, with the V4 we would take some special initiatives to create an annual business forum. As foreign ministers, we would meet annually-that was the consensus," Jaishankar said. He said India and the V4 countries would also explore greater cooperation in technology and innovation, while seeking to strengthen existing defence ties. "We have a very strong history with all the V4 countries in defence. We want to refresh and take forward that record and that cooperation," the External Affairs Minister said. Jaishankar said the discussions covered space, connectivity and people-to-people mobility, noting that Indian students are present in each of the V4 countries. The meeting also saw an exchange of views on major global developments, including the Ukraine conflict and the situation in the Gulf. "So, overall, I can tell you in terms of our cooperation, as well as a very good exchange-a very useful exchange on the big global crises: the Ukraine conflict, what's happening in the Gulf," Jaishankar said. In a separate post on X, Jaishankar said the meeting agreed to closer political cooperation, deeper economic engagement, stronger technology, innovation, research and education partnerships, reinvigorated defence cooperation and expanded cultural and people-to-people relations. Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanar said the V4 countries supported India's permanent membership of the UN Security Council. "We all agree as V4 countries that India as a part of the Global South, upcoming superpower in the Indo-Pacific region, must be at the table as the permanent member of the UN Security Council," Blanar said. Jaishankar also held bilateral meetings with French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot and Ecuadorian Foreign Minister Roberto Kury during his UNGA engagements. https://www.budapesttimes.hu/diplomacy/m.text: The Budapest Times Magyar meets Pope Leo XIV in Rome The first stop of Prime Minister Péter Magyar and his delegation during their Vatican visit was the Hungarian chapel in St. Peter's Basilica, from where they proceeded to the Apostolic Palace for a private audience with Pope Leo XIV on Thursday. Péter Magyar arrived in the Apostolic Palace’s inner courtyard, known as the Courtyard of San Damaso, a few minutes after half past ten, where an honour guard of the Swiss Guard was lined up. The Prime Minister was received at the entrance to the Apostolic Palace by Archbishop Peter Rajic, Prefect of the Papal Household, along with the papal court dignitaries who escorted Péter Magyar and his delegation all the way to the papal library. Following the private audience, the Prime Minister proceeded to the Secretariat of State of the Holy See, where he held talks with Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, known as the Vatican’s foreign minister, as well as with Father Fabio Salerno, who is also responsible for Hungarian affairs at the Holy See. The Hungarian delegation includes Zoltán Tarr, Minister for Social Relations and Culture; György Velkey, Parliamentary State Secretary of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs; and István Czeti, Deputy State Secretary for Church Affairs. The Prime Minister’s Vatican visit began in the Hungarian chapel located in the crypt of St. Peter’s Basilica. Péter Magyar entered the basilica through the so-called Gate of Prayer, a bronze gate reserved for heads of state and government. The Hungarian chapel is located in the basilica’s crypt, near the tombs of the Apostle Peter and the popes. It was consecrated by John Paul II in October 1980 as a legacy of the former Hungarian pilgrimage house founded by Saint Stephen. The Chapel of the Great Lady of the Hungarians is adorned with works by Hungarian artists, featuring reliefs depicting Hungarian saints. A statue of Saint Stephen stands at the altar, holding the holy crown. The Hungarian-language Mass was celebrated by Gergő Eredics, Deputy Office Director of the Archdiocesan Office. At the end of his homily, he emphasised that the common thread among Hungarian saints and blesseds is that they heard the word of God and translated it into action. Father Eredics recalled Sára Salkaházy, beatified in 2006, and Mária Magdolna Bódi, beatified in 2025. The concelebrant Viktor Zsódi, Provincial Superior of the Hungarian province of the Piarist order, spoke of the fearless witness borne by Hungarian saints, marking the feast day of Bishop and Martyr Saint Gerard. He stressed that Saint Gerard’s motto was “do not be afraid” — “he lived by it, he was not afraid to bear witness.” He cited the counsel of Cardinal Carlo Maria Martini as an example of how witness can be given in today’s world. https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.text: Illustration: Anaïs Mims/Guardian Design View image in fullscreen Illustration: Anaïs Mims/Guardian Design The long read Germany A death, a plagiarism scandal and a quest for revenge: the bizarre tale of Otto Z After his mother died, Otto became convinced he’d been wronged by the forensic investigators – and that one of them was a fraud. The truth was even stranger Alessio Perrone Thu 8 Oct 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 06.23 EDT Share On a balmy, quiet evening in June 2020, Otto’s elderly mother, Doria, was fading in her Munich apartment. As she lay with her eyes closed, her pale face, framed by her white hair, was calm. Otto, masked, gloved and draped in a sterile apron, dozed in a chair beside her. Otto, who sometimes goes by the name Rainer, and whose last name is only known as “Z” because of Germany’s strict privacy laws, was a doctor who had cared for his mother for years, ever since she had suffered a stroke and moved in with him. He described the course of that night to me. He woke to the sound of her short breath and tried to sit her upright. Her eyes were shut, and her lips pursed. She stopped breathing. Otto reached for his phone to call for help, but then Doria opened her eyes and stared into his. She smiled, drew one last deep breath, shut her eyes again, and lay still. Otto sank into his chair. As a doctor, he had seen death many times, but his own mother’s passing sent him into shock. He felt frozen, watching the windows glisten in the fading light. He was 66, and his brother and father had died years before. He had no friends. He had given all of his time, energy and attention to his mother’s care, and now that his task was suddenly over, he had no one to turn to. He mourned in solitude, with an impromptu ritual. He lit candles and set metal plates at the four corners of her bed. He sat beside her and thought about her soul. Once the rite was complete, Otto picked up the phone and called a funeral home. He knew the procedure: as a doctor, he could issue his own mother’s death certificate. After he hung up, Otto waited. It was the last calm moment he would experience for many months. After he called the funeral home, Otto told me, he waited beside his mother all night and into the next afternoon before he heard a knock at the door. He was surprised to see that, rather than doctors, the two men in the hallway were police officers. They wore bulletproof vests and carried guns. He invited them inside, where they scanned the rooms. He directed them to his mother’s bedroom and followed close behind, but the officers stopped him and asked him to take a seat. While the officers inspected his mother’s body, Otto sat in his office. Forty-five minutes passed, and then he heard someone else enter the flat without knocking. A tall, stylish woman approached and introduced herself as a coroner from the Munich Institute of Forensic Medicine, before walking off to the bedroom. Otto knew that a coroner – as opposed to a doctor or nurse – is only sent to the scenes of suspicious deaths. He followed her to the bedroom, where she had begun inspecting his mother’s body. Otto wasn’t easily rattled, but he told me that the way the coroner handled Doria threw him off. He found her elegant attire unprofessional, given the circumstances, and her bedside manner lacking. He said that he tried, however, to remain polite and helpful. As she went about her work, he offered his recollections from his mother’s final hours and an account of her long illness, which he had documented minutely over the years. Otto informed the coroner that he was a doctor, but it seemed to him that she was uninterested. She turned to the police officers and, without explanation, told them that this was a matter for law enforcement, before leaving the flat. Otto told me he wondered why nobody was listening to him, the grieving son, the doctor? More armed police officers arrived and searched the rooms. A commissioner approached Otto and told him to gather his things, as they needed to conduct their work uninterrupted. Sleep-deprived and grief-stricken, Otto was ushered on to the street and ordered not to return. He drifted along Munich’s wide, lamplit streets. As darkness fell upon the city, Otto told me he felt that he “didn’t understand the world any more”. He checked into a hotel, but found it intolerable to sit in his room. Later that night he wandered back to his flat and found the door sealed with police tape. He was desperate to check in on his mother and thought she might still be inside. He broke the police seal and entered the dark rooms, which were a chaotic mess, as if burglars had turned it over before fleeing the scene. He entered the bedroom. His mother was gone. Otto went back to his hotel but still found it impossible to sleep. He returned to his flat a second time at about 2am, and this time he found several police officers stationed there. They spotted him and put him in the back of a police car. He was taken to the Institute of Forensic Medicine, where doctors extracted samples from him: hair, urine and blood. When they had finished, Otto was taken back to the police station and found himself alone in what he described as a tiny, windowless cell with only a mattress, a stainless steel toilet and bars on the door. The next morning, two officers questioned him. How did he care for Doria? Why did he document her condition so precisely? Had he given his mother a concentrated saline injection? Only then did Otto understand: the police believed he had murdered his mother. After two nights in jail, or possibly three (his memory of this time is confused), Otto was released and allowed to return to his flat. While it was a relief to be home, he told me he still didn’t understand why he was under suspicion. He had not yet been formally charged with any crime. Otto wrote to the head of the Institute of Forensic Medicine, Prof Matthias Graw, to ask if his team had discovered anything suspicious while inspecting Doria’s body. Eager to prove his innocence, Otto offered to send Graw all of his day-to-day notes on Doria’s health. He suggested, boldly, that they co-author a paper about the cause of her death. Graw never answered Otto’s emails, and Otto fell into a depression. He told me he began blaming himself for his mother’s death. Had he made a mistake? Overlooked some critical detail? Was there some way he could have saved her? Over the years, he said, he had taken her to see 19 different specialists to ensure that she received the best care. He made sure she exercised and spent time each day in the fresh air. He had tried his best, hadn’t he? Doria was his whole world. Before the pandemic he used to take her into the city centre each night, where she was a favourite among the buskers for her generous tips. In her younger years, Doria had been an avid traveller, and Otto had taken her, in a wheelchair, on one last holiday to Italy. Now she was gone. Otto’s despair grew until he was unable to eat or sleep. In January 2021, the authorities dropped their investigation into his mother’s death, and Otto was cleared of any wrongdoing. But he still couldn’t get over her death. He checked himself into a psychiatric treatment centre, hoping to quiet his mind. Through therapy and exercise, Otto slowly regained his strength. Meanwhile, he had received a copy of the results of his mother’s toxicological report, signed by Graw and two of his institute’s specialists, but he was too disoriented to examine them carefully. Months passed. It was mid-summer, after Otto had moved back into his apartment, when he finally sat down with Doria’s medical files and the report. With two PhDs and decades of experience in medicine and chemistry, Otto knew how to interpret lab reports. He told me that something seemed off. Data seemed to him to have been highlighted selectively. Other details seemed to him to have been glossed over. In the toxicological report, he said he spotted a chemical compound – commonly associated with exposure to cold – in her bloodstream. In his telling, an impossible, unspeakable idea crept into his mind: could his mother have somehow still been alive when she was taken away and stowed in the mortuary’s freezer? Could she have actually died at the Institute of Forensic Medicine, under the coroner’s care? And if so, how? The report also mentioned unusual traces of a substance contained in the autumn crocus flower, a poison called colchicine. Otto began researching the Institute of Forensic Medicine. He started with its director, Prof Matthias Graw, and discovered that decades earlier, when Graw was a doctoral student at the University of Hamburg, he had written his dissertation on a certain naturally occurring poison found in the autumn crocus flower, called colchicine – the same poison found in Doria’s blood. Otto told me that a dark theory took shape in his mind: what if the institute had tried to frame him, to cover up the fact that they had actually killed his mother? He did not go to the police – who, he reasoned, must work closely with the head of the institute of legal medicine. He would take the matter into his own hands. Hoping to perform his own examinations, Otto again wrote to the institute and requested access to his mother’s remains. Once more, his letter received no reply. In his apartment, hunched over his computer, Otto dug deeper into Graw, looking for evidence of negligence or criminality in the records of the man who oversaw his mother’s autopsy. He scoured scientific literature to research colchicine, the poison in which Graw was an expert. By mid-February 2022, Otto had on his desk a book, dated 1982. Its title was Colchicine – 100 Years of Research . One of the chapters – its experiments, findings, tables and conclusion – was nearly identical to Graw’s dissertation, published five years later. Otto was convinced that he had in his hands the evidence he needed to bring Graw down. At the end February 2022, a man named Stefan Weber was sitting in his office on the outskirts of Salzburg when an intriguing email landed in his inbox. The message claimed that Graw, the head of the Institute of Forensic Medicine at the University of Munich and one of the most respected forensic scientists in Germany, had plagiarised his doctoral thesis. View image in fullscreen Stefan Weber, a plagiarism hunter. Photograph: Joachim Bergauer This was the kind of message Weber lived for. Fifty-six years old, baby-faced, broad, energetic and unrelentingly serious, Weber is the German-speaking world’s most-feared plagiarism hunter. His investigations have previously targeted Austria’s former labour and family minister Christine Aschbacher, who stepped down after Weber claimed her master’s thesis showed “never-before-seen depths of gobbledegook, nonsense and plagiarism”, and the German politician Annalena Baerbock, whose once-promising bid for the chancellorship was torpedoed when he investigated her book. The New York Times has called Weber the “undisputed terror of academics, politicians, [and] celebrities”. Weber does not go out of his way to be liked. A former communications professor, he failed on eight occasions at eight universities to attain tenure. His colleagues in academia often found him brusque and inflexible. He told me he was hated because of his insistence on high standards. Weber dresses in black and conducts his affairs with extreme scrupulousness. Fearing diabetes, he fasts for long periods. He spends his days in almost complete solitude, moving between his office, the library and the copy shop. He receives numerous requests for investigations each month, mostly from law firms and private individuals who want him to look into an applicant, competitor or colleague. Weber told me he charges up to €350 an hour for his work. He frequently pillories both public figures and obscure academics on his blog, where he also rails against “the Wokistan ideology ” and has written: “ Rightwing extremist must be understood as a title of honour!” In his spare time, he writes lofty books of philosophy and theory, with titles such as Language, Humanity, Universe. The email, sent by one Otto Z, claimed that Graw’s entire career was “built on deception”. From Otto’s description, the colchicine book would have been an easy source to pilfer. It had been published in East Germany at the height of the cold war, which meant that it most likely wasn’t known to western academics when Graw published his dissertation. It was also, in plagiarism-hunter parlance, “grey literature”: informal material that isn’t peer-reviewed and therefore lies outside the reach of digital research platforms. Without Otto’s tip-off, it would have been impossible for Weber to discover the book’s existence. Weber accepted the case and, with the help of an assistant, got to work researching the book. The archive of the East German publisher had been lost after reunification, and the book had never been cited by another source. Weber went searching for a physical copy. At the library, the elderly archivist told him they didn’t carry it. After consulting her databases, she informed him that no other library in the world did, either. But she found a single copy on eBay, for $220, and soon Weber held the book in his hands: a bright red hardcover. When Weber sat down to read it, he discovered that the red book told an incredible story nearly lost to history. It was a record of an academic symposium held in 1981 at a hospital in the small Romanian city of Târgu Neamţ. Present were eminent experts on colchicine – biologists, pharmacists, zoologists – who gathered to present their work. Their lectures and conversations were assembled into chapters that chronicled the history of their niche field of research. Since at least the first century, the autumn crocus has been known to be toxic. Since the sixth century, the toxin responsible, colchicine, has been used to treat gout. Throughout the 20th century, new uses for colchicine were discovered: its ability to disrupt microtubules, for example, helps scientists study cell division, disease mechanisms and drug toxicity. More surprising than any discovery presented at the symposium, however, was the guest list. Experts came from both sides of the iron curtain. At least two Americans were present: zoologist John Julius Biesele and obesity researcher Jules Hirsch. Had these westerners risked their reputations, careers and possibly their freedom to take part? Perhaps the explanation had something to do with the symposium’s host, Elena Ceaușescu, the eccentric and ruthless wife of Nicolae Ceaușescu, then-dictator of Romania. Adding a bizarre twist to Weber’s investigation, Mrs Ceaușescu was, herself, an infamous academic cheat . Despite only completing elementary school, she believed that she was “born a great chemist”, and coerced the Polytechnic Institute in Bucharest into awarding her a PhD in chemistry. Throughout her husband’s reign, she forced Romanian chemists to produce work under her name. Had she somehow blackmailed western scientists into attending her conference? Or could they have been spies sent by the CIA to gather intelligence? When Romania’s Soviet-backed regime collapsed in 1989, Elena Ceaușescu, along with her husband, was executed by firing squad. Weber’s research turned up no other references to her groundbreaking conference. By 2022, most of its attendants had also passed away. The conference seemed destined to remain a footnote in the history of science. But poring over the pages of Colchicine, Weber was soon convinced that one man had not overlooked the book: Matthias Graw. After cross-referencing the red book and Graw’s dissertation, Weber and his assistant concluded that nearly 80% of Graw’s work was not original. Two of his thesis’s central chapters and many whole sections were word-for-word copies, with images and tables reproduced wholesale. On 6 June 2022, Weber finally filed his report .
